content.title: About
content.content: Baby toddler prunes are natural dried plum fruits specially processed without added sugar or preservatives. They are soft, easy to chew, and suitable for children from 1 year old. Prunes are rich in vitamins, minerals, and dietary fiber that support healthy development.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Plums belong to the rose family, along with cherries, peaches, and apricots.
Dried prunes have been a staple in infant nutrition in Europe and Asia for centuries.
Natural sugars in dried prunes are higher than in fresh fruit, but no extra sugar is added.
Prunes are one of the richest sources of vitamin K among dried fruits.
When properly processed, prunes retain most of the antioxidants found in fresh plums.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immunity, and cell growth in children.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immune defense and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps prevent constipation in toddlers.

items.title: Potassium for heart health
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some children may be allergic to plums; discontinue use if any reaction occurs.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although natural, the sugar can contribute to dental caries in children prone to cavities.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Dry prunes should be pre‑soaked or cut into small pieces for children under 3 years.

items.title: Stomach discomfort
items.content: Large amounts may cause gastrointestinal upset due to high sugar concentration.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Give small pieces of dried prunes after soaking them in warm water for 10–15 minutes to soften. They can be added to oatmeal, yogurt, purees, or used as a natural sweetener in toddler desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried prunes in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. For longer shelf life keep them in the refrigerator. Discard any prunes that show mold, off‑odors, or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Bacon is smoked or cured pork, typically taken from the belly or back of the pig. In the US, the NS (No Sugar) label indicates a version without added sugar, usually prepared by grilling or baking. Bacon is known for its distinctive aroma, crisp texture, and rich meaty flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bacon dates back to ancient Rome, where it was called "petaso".
Americans consume more than 12 million tons of bacon each year.
The word "bacon" comes from Old French "bacon", meaning "pork".
Bacon is a staple in culinary contests, such as competitions for the crispiest strips.
In some US regions, bacon is served with maple syrup as a traditional breakfast.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Bacon provides about 12 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for normal blood formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Provides selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Bacon quickly supplies the body with energy due to its high fat content.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Large amounts of salt can raise blood pressure and strain the kidneys.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Excessive intake of saturated fats is linked to increased cardiovascular risk.

items.title: Nitrites and nitrates
items.content: Curing often uses nitrites, which at high levels can form potentially carcinogenic compounds.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork proteins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bacon can be pan‑fried, baked in the oven, or grilled until crisp. It is used in breakfasts, salads, sandwiches, pastas, and as a flavor enhancer for vegetable dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bacon in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a zip‑lock bag for up to 6 months. Before use, check for off‑smell or gray discoloration; discard if any signs of spoilage are present.

beef-with-vegetable-diet-frozen-meal.title: Beef with vegetable, diet frozen meal

content.title: About
content.content: Beef with vegetable is a ready‑to‑heat frozen meal designed for diet nutrition. It contains lean beef, a mix of carrots, broccoli, cauliflower and other vegetables, plus herbs without added fats or sugars. The dish can be microwaved in 3–4 minutes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: One serving provides more than 30 % of the daily protein requirement.
Vegetables are flash‑blanched to retain most of their vitamins.
Beef is sourced from verified suppliers that do not use growth hormones.
Freezing occurs within 30 minutes after cooking, preserving flavor.
Each package is a single portion (≈250 g).

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Protein is essential for maintaining muscle mass and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Lean beef and the absence of added fats make the meal suitable for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef provides vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: The vegetable mix supplies dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish contains iron, zinc and potassium, important for immunity and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Allergy to beef or vegetables
items.content: People with known food allergies should check the ingredient list before consumption.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Those limiting salt should monitor the sodium level indicated on the package.

items.title: Requires thorough heating
items.content: Insufficiently heated product may contain live bacteria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the frozen meal in the microwave on high power for 3–4 minutes, stir, and let stand for 1 minute. Optionally garnish with fresh herbs or a squeeze of lemon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen meal at –18 °C or lower. After thawing, consume within 2 hours and do not store in the refrigerator for more than 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: The beef, bean and cheese burrito is a classic Mexican dish consisting of a large wheat tortilla wrapped around a filling of sautéed beef, cooked beans, shredded cheese, and often additional vegetables and spices. The combination provides protein, fiber, and calcium, making it a balanced meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Burritos originated in northern Mexico where wheat flour was more available than corn.
Traditional fillings use black beans, but red or pinto beans are also common.
Beef is usually seasoned with cumin, paprika, and chili for a distinctive flavor.
Cheese in Mexican cuisine is often cheddar or queso fresco, which melts nicely when heated.
Burritos are frequently served with salsa, guacamole, and sour cream to adjust spiciness and creaminess.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef and beans provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Fiber from beans
items.content: Beans contain soluble and insoluble fiber that supports healthy digestion and blood‑sugar stability.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Shredded cheese supplies calcium, important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef is high in vitamin B12, while beans provide folate, both supporting the nervous system and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Cumin and chili contain antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces or salty cheeses can raise sodium levels, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Beef and cheese can be high in saturated fat; choosing lean cuts and moderating cheese helps keep fat intake reasonable.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or dairy allergy should substitute cheese with a plant‑based alternative.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Burritos are calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Burritos are hand‑held; cut them in half for easier handling. Warm them in a microwave or skillet until the cheese melts. Top with fresh salsa, guacamole, or sour cream to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared burrito in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, wrap tightly in plastic film and freeze for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Carrot (Daucus carota) is a root vegetable believed to have originated in the region of present-day Iran and Afghanistan. It is best known for its crisp texture and sweet, earthy flavor. Although orange carrots are the most familiar, carrots also come in purple, yellow, red, and white varieties. Both the root and the leafy tops are edible.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Early cultivated carrots were often purple or yellow; orange varieties became widespread in Europe later.
The orange color comes mainly from beta-carotene, a pigment the body can convert into vitamin A.
Wild carrot, also known as Queen Anne's lace, is the ancestor of the cultivated carrot.
Carrots are rich in natural sugars, which is why they taste sweeter when cooked or roasted.
Carrot greens are edible and can be used in pesto, soups, and salads.

items.title: Rich in beta-carotene
items.content: The body converts beta-carotene into vitamin A, which supports normal vision, skin, and immune function.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Carrots contribute fiber that supports normal digestion.

items.title: Contains vitamin K and potassium
items.content: Carrots provide vitamin K1, which supports normal blood clotting, and potassium, which helps maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids and other plant compounds help protect cells against oxidative damage.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Carrots are filling and low in calories, making them a convenient snack.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some people, especially those allergic to birch pollen, may experience itching or tingling in the mouth after eating raw carrots.

items.title: Carotenemia
items.content: Very large amounts of carrots or carrot juice over time may cause a harmless yellow-orange tint of the skin.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Raw carrot pieces can be a choking hazard for small children and should be grated, cooked, or cut appropriately.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Eating a lot of fiber at once may cause bloating in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Carrots can be eaten raw as a snack, grated into salads, or dipped in hummus. They can be boiled, steamed, roasted, or added to soups, stews, pilafs, and baked goods. Eating carrots with a little fat, such as olive oil, may improve the absorption of carotenoids.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Remove the leafy tops and store carrots in the refrigerator, in a perforated bag or container, where they can keep for several weeks. Keep them away from ripening fruit. Peeled or cut carrots should be kept in an airtight container and eaten within a few days. Carrots can also be blanched and frozen.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-potatoe.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with potatoes and/or onions, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of eggs cooked together with potatoes and/or onions, with added vegetable or butter fat. Eggs provide high‑quality protein, while potatoes and onions supply carbohydrates, fiber, and vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs can be prepared as a fluffy omelet (whisked) or as scrambled eggs (not whisked).
Potatoes are usually diced or sliced and either boiled or fried before mixing with the eggs.
Onion adds aroma and contains compounds that support heart health.
Adding fat increases calorie content but improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins from the vegetables.
Traditionally the dish is cooked in a non‑stick skillet.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Eggs contain all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and potatoes provide vitamin B12, B6, and folate, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Potassium and magnesium
items.content: Potatoes and onions are good sources of potassium and magnesium, which help normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Onion supplies quercetin, and egg yolk provides lutein, both protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Improved nutrient absorption
items.content: Fat aids the body in absorbing fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K found in eggs and vegetables.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white proteins.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: The added fat and potatoes make the dish energy‑dense; portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolk contains cholesterol; people with elevated cholesterol levels should limit yolk intake.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Over‑cooking potatoes can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Sauté diced potatoes and onions in a small amount of fat until golden. In a bowl, whisk eggs with salt and pepper, then pour over the vegetables in the skillet. Cook, stirring, until the desired consistency is reached. Garnish with herbs if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The dish is best eaten fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours; reheat in a skillet or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: French toast sticks are a ready‑to‑eat product consisting of long bread sticks that are dipped in a mixture of eggs, milk, cinnamon and sugar, then baked or fried until crisp. They are convenient for school or on‑the‑go meals, serving as a quick breakfast or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The classic French toast recipe originated in France in the 19th century as a way to use stale bread.
Sticks are created by cutting the toast into strips before cooking, making them child‑friendly.
There are many variations: vanilla, berry, nut, or chocolate‑glazed versions are common.
In the United States, they are often served with maple syrup or fruit sauces.
The sticks can be frozen and reheated in a microwave while retaining their crunch.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Eggs in the batter provide a modest amount of complete protein, supporting growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Milk adds calcium, important for bone and tooth development, especially in children.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: French toast sticks supply B1, B2 and B6 vitamins that help with energy metabolism.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: When made with whole‑grain bread, they provide fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates and a small amount of fat offers a quick source of energy for active students.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sticks are often sweetened, so they should be eaten in moderation, especially by children at risk for cavities.

items.title: Egg or milk allergy
items.content: The product may trigger allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to eggs or dairy proteins.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because of the oil used for cooking, the sticks can be calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Crunchiness hazard
items.content: Hard, crunchy sticks can break teeth in very young children, so supervision is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the sticks as a standalone snack, dip them in maple syrup, fruit sauce, yogurt, or nut butter. They fit easily into a lunchbox and can be quickly reheated in a microwave if needed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed package in a cool, dry place. After opening, consume within 3–5 days or store in the refrigerator to maintain crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanuts are legumes whose seeds are commonly called nuts. Roasted salted peanuts have a distinctive aroma, crunchy texture, and a lightly salty flavor. They are enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, baked goods, and Asian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanuts belong to the legume family, not true nuts.
They are cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions, with the United States, India, and China as the top producers.
Two main roasting methods are dry roasting and oil roasting.
Peanuts are a source of vegetable oil used to make peanut oil and margarine.
In the U.S., roasted salted peanuts are a classic snack often seasoned with sea salt.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Peanuts contain about 25 % protein, making them a good plant‑based protein source.

items.title: Unsaturated fats
items.content: Peanut fats are mainly mono‑ and polyunsaturated, supporting heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: They provide niacin, folate, and vitamin B6, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Peanuts supply magnesium, phosphorus, potassium, and iron, aiding muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Resveratrol and other phenolic compounds in peanuts help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanuts are one of the most common food allergens and can cause severe reactions.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because of their fat content, peanuts are calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: The salted version can contribute to elevated blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Aflatoxins
items.content: Improper storage can lead to aflatoxin formation, so purchase from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peanuts can be eaten straight from the bag, added to salads, soups, sauces, baked goods, and Asian recipes. They are also processed into peanut butter, pastes, and flour.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store roasted salted peanuts in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them refrigerated to prevent oil rancidity.
